title: Off-policy Learning with Excursion Policies
claim: A toy example shows that multi-step excursions beat step-wise mixtures when switching is costly, because mixtures oscillate between policies.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right: MDP schematic then two line plots, shared legend
description: The figure has three panels. On the left is a schematic of a highway MDP. It has an initial circle node that branches into a top fast lane (F1 to F3 to a red terminal T_B) and a bottom slow lane (S1 to S3 to a green terminal T_A). Black arrows carry small red reward labels: +1.0 and -15.0 on the fast lane, +0.01 on the slow lane. Dashed grey diagonal arrows labeled c mark the lane-switching costs. The blue italic labels Left (π) and Right (μ) mark the first action. The middle and right panels are line plots of the initial-state value against an interpolation parameter (α or β). Purple is the mixture policy and orange is the excursion policy. Dashed green and blue horizontal lines show the π and μ baselines. Without switching cost, the mixture curve peaks higher than the excursion curve. With cost, the mixture dips far below the baselines while the excursion stays above them. A legend sits on the far right.
caption: Analysis of the Highway MDP example. Left: Schematic of the MDP featuring a "slow lane" (reward $0.01$, destination $T_A$) and a "fast lane" (reward $1.0$, terminal penalty $-15.0$ at $T_B$). The discount factor $\gamma$ is $0.9$. Middle and Right: Value of the initial state under various policies without switching costs $c=0$ (middle) and with a cost of $c=-1.0$ (right), both based on an extended $10$-state chain. The behavior policy $\mu$ prefers the safe slow lane, while the target policy $\pi$ prefers the fast lane. This example illustrates that a one-time excursion policy ($\expolicy^\exvar$) can be better than a mixture policy ($\alphapolicy^\alpha$) when lane-switching incurs a penalty, as the latter induces frequent, costly oscillations.
abstract: Off-policy reinforcement learning (RL) tries to learn the value of a target policy while data comes from a different behavior policy. This often requires trading off bias for variance or stability. One way to trade these off is to linearly interpolate between the behavior and target policies, but this represents only one point in a broader space of interpolation mechanisms. We introduce excursion policies--a structured alternative where the agent follows the target policy for a multi-step "excursion" before reverting to the behavior policy. We derive dynamic programming results for these policies, establishing the theoretical basis for their use in RL. We further develop provably sound off-policy temporal-difference (TD) algorithms for excursion value estimation. We find that excursion policies provide an efficiency-stability trade-off comparable to mixture policies in continuous control benchmarks, and our analysis illustrates conceptual differences in their behavior.
